system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2147-09-25 16:28:00 to 2147-09-28 15:35:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of polymyositis, morbid obesity, type 2 diabetes, and chronic venous thromboembolism was admitted for progressive shortness of breath and an 80-pound weight gain over several months. She was diagnosed with acute on chronic diastolic heart failure, likely due to fluid overload, despite a low BNP, which can be falsely low in obesity. She responded well to intravenous furosemide and was transitioned to oral furosemide 60 mg twice daily. A right heart catheterization showed normal pressures, likely due to prior diuresis, supporting heart failure as the primary cause. She was also treated for an asymptomatic Enterococcus urinary tract infection with a five-day course of ampicillin. Obstructive sleep apnea was addressed with BiPAP initiation, which improved her sleep quality. Her supratherapeutic INR on admission led to temporary holding of warfarin and bridging with heparin during the catheterization; she was discharged on warfarin 10 mg daily with INR of 2.1. Her polymyositis was stable without flare, and anemia was noted as stable with iron studies ordered for outpatient follow-up. She was discharged home with instructions to monitor daily weights, continue BiPAP, and follow up with cardiology, pulmonary, rheumatology, and primary care.
problems: Acute on chronic diastolic heart failure
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

Discharge Instructions:
It was a pleasure caring for you at ___. You were admitted 
because there was some concern that you may have a lung 
infection referred to as pneumonia. It was determined that you 
did not have pneumonia, and instead believe that your cough, 
body aches, and congestion were due to a cold. 

We believe that some of your shortness of breath was due to your 
heart failure worsening. We treated you with diuretics through 
your veins in order for you lose fluid through your urine. Your 
weight was chacked and it was noted that you lost 9 pounds in 
water weight overnight. On the day of discharge you denied any 
shortness of breath.

Please weigh yourself at home and refer to your PCP for weight 
gain >3 lbs.

PLEASE NOTE, THE FOLLOWING CHANGES WERE MADE TO YOUR MEDICATIONS
-STOP lasix
-START torsemide 80 mg by mouth daily
-START ferrous gluconate 325 mg daily
 
Followup Instructions:
___

FINDINGS:  Study is limited due to patient body habitus.  Diffuse interstitial
opacity appears similar compared to prior.  No new focal consolidation or
pneumothorax is detected.  Heart size is top normal and unchanged.

IMPRESSION:  Diffuse interstitial abnormality, similar compared to prior.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You came in today because of shortness of breath and cold-like symptoms. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had a cough for about a week, with yellow mucus, stuffy nose, body aches, and a low fever. My regular doctor thought I might have pneumonia, so she sent me here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how’s your breathing been? Any worse at night or when lying down?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m short of breath, but not worse at night. I’ve been using my CPAP at home, which helps me rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We also noticed you’ve gained about 10 pounds since your last admission. Are you following your fluid and salt restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I try, but I did have some canned pasta sauce and fries last week. I didn’t think it was that bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those are high in sodium, which can cause fluid retention and make your heart work harder. That’s likely why your breathing got worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize. So it’s not just the cold making me short of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Both are playing a role. The cold is causing congestion, but the fluid buildup from heart failure is making it harder to breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What will we do about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a diuretic through your IV to help your body get rid of the extra fluid. We’ll also monitor your breathing and do a chest X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows changes similar to what you’ve had before from your lung disease. No new pneumonia, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t have pneumonia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it looks like a viral upper respiratory infection—basically a bad cold. We’ll hold off on antibiotics since they won’t help with viruses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I had a fever and yellow mucus. I thought that meant infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yellow mucus can happen with colds too. Since you’re not getting worse and your X-ray is clear, we think it’s viral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your blood. One culture came back positive, but since you don’t have signs of infection, we think it’s a lab contaminant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. A second culture was negative, so we won’t treat it. It’s common and not a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your weight is down by 4 pounds already from the diuretic. How’s your breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I feel less tight in my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep giving you the diuretic to help lose more fluid. We also want to adjust your home medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s changing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching from furosemide to torsemide. It works better in people with heart failure and is more reliable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, so I’ll take that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one pill a day. And we’re starting you on iron pills because your blood count is low from iron deficiency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is it worse now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s stable. But we want to treat it to help your energy and overall health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was a bit high when you came in—3.4—so we held your warfarin for a day. It’s back to 2.6 now, so we’ve restarted it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’m on it for my blood clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we monitor it closely. A high INR increases bleeding risk, so we adjust carefully. You’re back on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve lost 9 pounds total and your breathing is much improved. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using your CPAP every night. Weigh yourself daily and call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t usually weigh myself. Should I start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s important. Sudden weight gain means fluid is building up, and we want to catch it early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stop furosemide and take torsemide once daily. Also, start the iron pill. All your other meds stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my rheumatology meds? I’m on prednisone and Cellcept.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue those. Your muscle enzyme levels are stable, so no flare of your polymyositis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. A nurse will come by to go over your meds and diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better. I’ll stick to low-salt food and keep using my CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Follow up with your PCP in a week and your cardiologist soon after. Call if you have trouble breathing or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay healthy.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of polymyositis, morbid obesity, type 2 diabetes, chronic venous thromboembolism, interstitial lung disease, and diastolic heart failure was admitted for worsening shortness of breath and URI symptoms one week after a prior discharge. She had gained 10 pounds, attributed to poor adherence to a low-sodium diet, and was treated with intravenous diuretics. Her respiratory symptoms were determined to be from a viral upper respiratory infection, not pneumonia, and antibiotics were withheld. She improved with diuresis, losing 9 pounds, and was transitioned from furosemide to torsemide for better bioavailability. Iron therapy was started for iron deficiency anemia, and warfarin was held briefly for an elevated INR before being safely restarted. She was discharged home with improved symptoms, instructions to monitor daily weights, and follow-up plans with her PCP and specialists.
